# Style guide: flat 2D folk-art cutout

## Look
- Minimalist flat 2D vector illustration inspired by Indian folk art (Madhubani, Pattachitra, miniature painting), simplified for digital media.
- Pure flat colour, no outlines anywhere: shapes are separated only by contrasting fills, plus one darker tone on the shadow side and a soft ground shadow under each figure. Characters are geometric cut-outs: square hair block framing a squared face, long heavy-lidded almond eyes with a thick brow, straight tapering limbs with flat ends, bead strands (necklace, armbands) and a wide diagonal sash. Set `FOLK_OUTLINE=soft` or `ink` to bring outlines back.
- Lighting is flat. Use soft radial glows and sunburst rays for key moments only.

## Palette
- Backgrounds: midnight blue and deep purple night skies; warm cream or saffron for day scenes.
- Hero characters: gold and saffron clothing. Divine or heroic figures get azure blue (Krishna) or radiant gold (Karna, armor).
- Accents: emerald green for nature and mountains, royal crimson and gold for kings and gods, muted ochre and white for disguised or humble figures.
- Keep 4-5 dominant colors per scene so the frame stays graphic.

## Motion
- Puppet-style cutout rigging: pivot at neck, shoulders and elbows. Add small blink and breathing loops on idle characters.
- Ease-in / ease-out on everything. No linear motion.
- Characters and props slide in from the sides or drop from above. Transitions are slides and wipes.
- A few frame-by-frame elements (rain, fire, sparks) add variety against the rigged characters.
- Fixed vertical 9:16 camera with gentle slow zooms. No shaky cam.
- Pacing: a new visual every 3-5 seconds.

## Text
- Devanagari subtitles at the top of the frame, a short phrase at a time, synced to the voice.
- Key words (names, numbers, the payoff word) get a scale-pop with ease-out.
- Counters, clocks and bead rings are built from shape layers and fill up in sync with the narration when math or counting is part of the story.

## Sound
- Strong, clear Hindi storyteller voiceover (deep male by default; ask if the user prefers otherwise).
- Subtle ambience matched to the scene (rain, wind, temple bells).
- Whoosh on slides, click or tick on counters, a chime on the big reveal.
- Soft sitar / flute / bell bed that ducks under the voice.

## Structure patterns that worked in the reference reel
- Hook that sets an open question over a thinking character.
- Story told as a small piece of logic or math the viewer can follow (e.g. 8 meals x 7 days = 56).
- Payoff scene that resolves the hook, then a paper-plane / follow-button CTA animation.


## Character design: each role must look different
Do not use one generic puppet for every character. Design from role and story:
- Hanuman/vanara: unmistakable vanara features and tail; gada only when appropriate; distinct face and silhouette.
- Devas: individual crowns, ornaments, skin palettes, garments and symbolic attributes; not identical royal puppets.
- Sages: age cues, jata/beard, simple robes and staff; no warrior armour.
- Kings/warriors: differentiated armour, weapons, headwear and body builds.
- Ordinary people: regional garments, practical accessories, varied ages and proportions.
Build a named character sheet before scene design. Keep each design consistent across the whole film.

## Caption treatment
Use concise, natural Devanagari captions. Prefer 3-8 words per card, one line where possible and no more than two. Use bold cream/white type with a restrained dark plum rounded plate, readable outline/shadow and generous padding. A single important word may use saffron/gold. Keep captions away from faces and key action. Do not shrink long sentences into tiny text; split them at natural spoken pauses. Proofread every line against the final script and inspect on a phone-sized preview.

## Reference reel lessons
The reference uses a vertical folk-art composition, clean dark caption plates near the top, high-contrast Devanagari and simple readable staging. Borrow the clarity and pacing, not its exact scenes or character designs.
